paraphrase: Most people follow the teaching 'while life lasts let one live happily; none escapes death; once the body is burnt to ashes, how can it return?'; the doctrine is well named Lokāyata ('the world-extended'), taught by Bṛhaspati and spread by Cārvāka, crest-jewel of the nāstikas.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, ch. 1 (Advaita doxography). Chapter-level ref; the Cārvāka chapter is not in the local DCS extract; recalled from the standard text. The first line uses the variant 'nāsti mṛtyor agocaraḥ', also in the Nyāyamañjarī.

paraphrase: The four elements are the principles; when they are transformed into a body, consciousness is produced as intoxicating power arises from kiṇva and other ingredients, and it perishes with them — the text cites 'arising from these elements it perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death' (BĀU 2.4.12). The self is the body qualified by consciousness, as shown by 'I am fat', 'I am thin', 'I am dark'; 'my body' is a figure of speech, like 'the head of Rāhu'.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, ch. 1 (Advaita doxography). Chapter-level ref; the Cārvāka chapter is not in the local DCS extract; recalled from the standard text.

paraphrase: Pleasure is the aim of life; if it is objected that pleasure is mixed with pain, the answer is that one takes the fish with its scales and bones, and the rice with its husk: 'who, seeking his good, would throw away rice rich in fine white grains because it is covered with husk?' — one does not stop sowing rice because there are deer, nor stop cooking because there are beggars.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, ch. 1 (Advaita doxography). Chapter-level ref; the Cārvāka chapter is not in the local DCS extract; recalled from the standard text.

paraphrase: Heaven is only the pleasure that comes from embracing women and the like; hell is the pain that comes from thorns and the like; the supreme lord is the king known to the world; liberation is the destruction of the body.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, ch. 1 (Advaita doxography). Chapter-level ref; the Cārvāka chapter is not in the local DCS extract; recalled from the standard text.

paraphrase: The agnihotra and the rest are only a means of livelihood; the Veda is tainted by falsehood, self-contradiction and repetition, and those who claim its authority refute one another, the followers of the works-section rejecting the knowledge-section and the reverse.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, ch. 1 (Advaita doxography). Chapter-level ref; the Cārvāka chapter is not in the local DCS extract; recalled from the standard text.

paraphrase: Perception is the only means of knowledge. Inference cannot be valid, because the invariable concomitance (vyāpti) on which it rests cannot be known: not by perception, which cannot reach all past and future instances, nor by inference, which would regress, nor by testimony or comparison; nor can one be sure that no adventitious condition (upādhi) is present. Success after an inference is accidental, like the success of gems, spells and drugs.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, ch. 1 (Advaita doxography). Chapter-level ref; the Cārvāka chapter is not in the local DCS extract; recalled from the standard text.

paraphrase: There is no unseen cause (adṛṣṭa): the variety of the world arises from own-nature (svabhāva) — 'fire is hot, water cold, the wind cool to the touch: by whom was this variety made? so it is fixed by their own nature'.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, ch. 1 (Advaita doxography). Chapter-level ref; the Cārvāka chapter is not in the local DCS extract; recalled from the standard text.

paraphrase: Verses ascribed to Bṛhaspati: there is no heaven, no liberation, no self in another world, and the rites of the classes and stages bear no fruit; the agnihotra, the three Vedas, the triple staff and smearing with ashes are a livelihood for those lacking intelligence and manliness; if a beast slain in the jyotiṣṭoma goes to heaven, why does the sacrificer not slay his own father? If the śrāddha satisfies the dead, then oil poured on an extinguished lamp would make its flame grow, and travellers need take no provisions; if offerings here satisfy those in heaven, why not feed those on the roof from below?

original.text: agnihotraṃ trayo vedās tridaṇḍaṃ bhasmaguṇṭhanam / buddhipauruṣahīnānāṃ jīviketi bṛhaspatiḥ // paśuś cen nihataḥ svargaṃ jyotiṣṭome gamiṣyati / svapitā yajamānena tatra kasmān na hanyate
original.edition: Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha ch. 1, vulgate (Abhyankar ed.); wording from memory, well known; variants exist
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted read-only for reference

notes: Reported by an opponent: the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, ch. 1 (Advaita doxography). Chapter-level ref; the Cārvāka chapter is not in the local DCS extract; recalled from the standard text. The first verse's last pāda has the variant 'jīvikā dhātṛnirmitā'. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa's Māyāmoha episode uses the sacrificed-animal argument too.

paraphrase: More verses: 'while life lasts let one live happily; let him drink ghee even on debt; once the body is burnt to ashes, how can it return?'; if the one who leaves the body went to another world, why does he not come back, drawn by love of his kin? The rites for the dead were devised by brāhmaṇas as a livelihood; the three makers of the Veda were buffoons, knaves and night-prowlers, and 'jarpharī turpharī' is the pandits' talk; the obscene rite of the aśvamedha and the eating of flesh were likewise laid down by them.

original.edition: Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha ch. 1, vulgate (Abhyankar ed.); wording from memory, well known; variants exist

paraphrase: The end of suffering is twofold: impersonal - the absolute destruction of all sufferings - and personal - lordship consisting in the powers of seeing and acting. The power of seeing is fivefold (seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing all treatises, omniscience); the power of acting threefold (swiftness of mind, taking forms at will, acting without organs).
notes: Opponent's / outsider's report: the Advaitin doxographer of the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, presenting the Pāśupata system in its own terms and quoting its authorities. Checked against the Muktabodha e-text M00508 of the Ganakarika with Ratnatika (C. D. Dalal ed., GOS 15, Baroda 1920) in sources_raw.

paraphrase: The dependent effect is threefold: vidyā (a quality of the paśu, cognitive or not), kalā (insentient, dependent on the sentient: ten 'effects' - five elements and five qualities - and thirteen 'instruments' - ten senses and the inner organs buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas), and paśu (with or without body and organs). Yoga is the link of self and Lord through the mind, either as action (muttering, meditation) or as cessation of action. The rule is primary (the observance: vows - ash-bathing, lying in ash, offering, muttering, circumambulation - and the six 'doors': krāthana, spandana, mandana, śṛṅgāraṇa, avitatkaraṇa, avitadbhāṣaṇa) or secondary (re-bathing etc.).
notes: Opponent's / outsider's report: the Advaitin doxographer of the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, presenting the Pāśupata system in its own terms and quoting its authorities. Checked against the Muktabodha e-text M00508 of the Ganakarika with Ratnatika (C. D. Dalal ed., GOS 15, Baroda 1920) in sources_raw.

paraphrase: The Pāśupatas claim five distinctions: elsewhere the end of suffering is only cessation, here it is also supreme lordship; elsewhere the effect comes to be, here soul and the rest are eternal; elsewhere the cause depends on something, here the Lord alone is independent; elsewhere yoga yields isolation, here supreme lordship and the end of suffering; elsewhere [heaven etc.] brings return, here the fruit is non-return, proximity and the like.
notes: Opponent's / outsider's report: the Advaitin doxographer of the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, presenting the Pāśupata system in its own terms and quoting its authorities. Checked against the Muktabodha e-text M00508 of the Ganakarika with Ratnatika (C. D. Dalal ed., GOS 15, Baroda 1920) in sources_raw.

paraphrase: Objection: if the Lord were an independent cause, karma would be fruitless and all effects would arise at once. Reply: karma favoured by the Lord's will bears fruit, and without it may be fruitless, as with Yayāti's; beings act because they depend on his will; he, whose desires are fulfilled, needs nothing that karma produces; and effects do not arise all at once, because his unimpeded power of action follows his will. As the knowers of the tradition say: 'Since he acts by his own will, independent of karma and the rest, he is called in scripture the cause of all causes.'

paraphrase: Liberation is not had from mere knowledge that Mahādeva is lord of the gods, nor can bound souls see him directly; right ascertainment of reality comes only from the Pāśupata scripture: 'In mere knowledge scripture suffices, but direct sight is hard to get; from nothing but the Pañcārtha comes true ascertainment of reality.'

paraphrase: Other Māheśvaras, though holding identity with the Supreme Lord, maintain that the jīvanmukti accepted by all will be accomplished only in stability of the body, and so proclaim rasa, called pārada, as the means — pārada because it carries one to the far shore (pāra) of saṃsāra. Liberation in life cannot be had any other way: all six systems place liberation after the fall of the body, where there can be no confidence in it and hence no undoubting effort.

original.text: saṃsārasya paraṃ pāraṃ datte'sau pāradaḥ smṛta iti

paraphrase: Many among gods, daityas, sages and men are said in the Raseśvara doctrine to have gained a divine body by the power of mercury and reached liberation in life: gods beginning with Maheśa, daityas led by Kāvya, sages like the Vālakhilyas, kings like Someśvara, Govinda Bhagavatpāda, Govindanāyaka, Carvaṭi, Kapila, Vyāli, Kāpāli, Kandalāyana and many other siddhas who, having gained a body made of mercury, roam liberated in life.
speaker: Mādhava, quoting the Raseśvarasiddhānta
notes: Rasa Śāstra (restricted): doctrine and warnings only; no procedures, quantities or recipes recorded.

paraphrase: How is the divine body achieved? Through the eighteen processings (saṃskāra) of mercury, which the teachers say must first be learned with effort by the wise; their details were set out by ancient teachers such as Govinda Bhagavatpāda and Sarvajña Rāmeśvara Bhaṭṭāraka and are passed over here for fear of length.
speaker: Mādhava (doxographer)
notes: Rasa Śāstra (restricted): doctrine and warnings only; no procedures, quantities or recipes recorded. The text lists the names of the eighteen processings; they are deliberately not reproduced here.

paraphrase: Rasa-śāstra is not to be thought to be only for metallurgy (dhātuvāda); its supreme purpose is liberation by way of transforming the body (dehavedha). The Rasārṇava: 'you gave me metal-transformation, lord; tell me body-transformation, by which the sky-going state may be' — 'as in metal, so in the body should mercury be applied by the good; it gives the same proof in body and metal: first test it on metal, afterward apply it to the body.'
speaker: Mādhava, quoting the Rasārṇava
notes: Rasa Śāstra (restricted): doctrine and warnings only; no procedures, quantities or recipes recorded. The 'test first on metal' rule is recorded as the tradition's own safety teaching.

paraphrase: Objection: liberation is accomplished by the manifestation of the supreme reality, being, consciousness and bliss — why this toil to produce a divine body? Reply: that is idle talk, for without a sound body there is no talk of it. The Rasahṛdaya: even when consciousness-bliss has flashed forth, what does it do for creatures to one whose body has not? A body worn by age is unfit for samādhi; a boy of sixteen is greedy for sense-pleasure, and the old man has lost discrimination — how can a mortal attain liberation?
speaker: Mādhava (doxographer)
notes: Rasa Śāstra (restricted): doctrine and warnings only; no procedures, quantities or recipes recorded.

paraphrase: Objection: living (jīvatva) means being in saṃsāra and liberation its opposite — how can they share one seat? Reply: liberation, accepted by all teachers, is either knowable or like a hare's horn; if knowable, life is not to be abandoned, for one who does not live cannot know. Nor is an eternal body unheard of: the followers of Viṣṇusvāmin establish the eternity of Nṛsiṃha's body, being, consciousness and bliss in form.
speaker: Mādhava (doxographer)
notes: Rasa Śāstra (restricted): doctrine and warnings only; no procedures, quantities or recipes recorded.

paraphrase: The body is the abode of all knowledge and the root of dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa; what higher good is there than an ageless, deathless body? Only the lord of rasas can make it so. Its greatness: fruit from seeing and touching it; worship of the mercurial liṅga is more auspicious than all the liṅgas of Kāśī and the rest; and the one who scorns mercury incurs sin and is to be abandoned.
speaker: Mādhava, quoting rasa texts
notes: Rasa Śāstra (restricted): doctrine and warnings only; no procedures, quantities or recipes recorded. Praise passage.

paraphrase: Therefore, having produced the divine body in the way stated, and seen the supreme reality by the power of yoga practice, one attains the goal of man: the conscious light between the brows, illumining the world like fire, lightning and sun, opens for some of meritorious vision — supreme bliss, of the nature of light, free of conception, peaceful, self-known; placing the mind in it and seeing the whole world as consciousness, one whose bonds of karma are cut attains brahmanhood here itself.
speaker: Mādhava, quoting the Rasahṛdaya
notes: Rasa Śāstra (restricted): doctrine and warnings only; no procedures, quantities or recipes recorded.

paraphrase: Scripture too says 'He is rasa; having obtained rasa one becomes blissful'; so it is established that rasa alone is the means of crossing the burden of suffering; a verse declares mercury's equality with the supreme brahman — may that mercury, which is brahman itself, protect us from the fear of wretched saṃsāra.
speaker: Mādhava (doxographer)
notes: Rasa Śāstra (restricted): doctrine and warnings only; no procedures, quantities or recipes recorded. Applies Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7 ('raso vai saḥ') to mercury.

paraphrase: Though the body of six sheaths is impermanent, the body born of the creation of Hara and Gaurī — called mercury and mica — can be permanent; so the yogin who seeks jīvanmukti must first make a divine body; mercury is Hara's and mica Gaurī's: 'mica is your seed, mercury mine; their union, O Goddess, destroys death and poverty.'
speaker: Mādhava (doxographer)
notes: Rasa Śāstra (restricted): doctrine and warnings only; no procedures, quantities or recipes recorded.
